subject: Inbound vs Egress: Choosing Peering, PrivateLink, or S2S for Private Deployments
messages:
From: Peter Zhao <peter.zhao@acme.example>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 9 Sep 2026 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: Connecting our VPC to Redwood Private — options question

Kim,

Quick context: we're evaluating Redwood Private for a pilot (private inference, on our VPC). Our security team has two non-negotiables: 1) no inbound public exposure to the inference hosts from the internet, and 2) we cannot accept cross-account routing that allows other AWS accounts to reach our VPC (that rules out simple peering in some org setups).

Given that, we wanted your recommendation between VPC Peering / PrivateLink / Site-to-Site VPN for production traffic (inference calls) and a separate management/control channel. The asks:
- Which option best meets isolation requirements while keeping latency low for our inference workloads?
- Any operational trade-offs we should prepare for (monitoring, failover, inter-region)?
- Is there a common pattern for combining two of these (e.g., PrivateLink for inference; S2S for management)?

Appreciate any notes or a short recommendation we can share with our infra/security folks.

Thanks,
Peter Zhao
Head of Cloud Engineering
Acme Logistics

Peter — thanks for the clear constraints. I'm going to loop in our infra and architecture leads for a short readout and proposal. High level from my side: PrivateLink is usually the right fit when customers need cross-account isolation plus AWS-managed endpoints; peering gives lowest latency when accounts are OK with routing; S2S is reliable for on-prem and egress-constrained setups but can add latency and operational overhead.

I'll send a short technical breakdown and a suggested pilot plan in the next message. Would you be available for a 30-min call tomorrow morning (PT) to walk through the proposal with your security team?

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
To: marcus_lin@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai, priyom_das@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 9 Sep 2026 14:00:00 -0700
Subject: FW: Connecting our VPC to Redwood Private — options question

Team — forwarding Acme's constraints. They explicitly call out: no internet-facing inference hosts, and no cross-account routing that would expose other AWS accounts to their VPC. Can you review the quick pros/cons below and suggest which pattern we should propose as our standard pilot for Acme? I want language the security team can sign off on.

Quick comparison (for inference traffic):
- VPC Peering: 
  - Pros: lowest network latency and simplest packet path (no NAT). Good for high-throughput, low-latency inference.
  - Cons: cross-account route propagation can be a policy blocker; scales poorly across many customers; no built-in AWS private service endpoint semantics.
- PrivateLink (AWS NLB + Endpoint Services):
  - Pros: cross-account isolation, customer controls endpoint in their VPC, traffic stays within AWS backbone, supports security boundary requirements. Scales well for multi-tenant hosted services; easier to audit/limit access.
  - Cons: slight latency overhead vs peering (NAT/encapsulation), health-check/socket limitations for certain protocols; costs for endpoint/data processed.
- Site-to-Site VPN / Direct Connect / Transit: 
  - Pros: works for on-prem or egress-only networks, can be encrypted and pinned to dedicated circuits, supports BGP for reachability.
  - Cons: higher and more variable latency, additional ops (BGP, rekeying), potential throughput limits per tunnel; adds more components to monitor.

Recommended baseline for Acme (given constraints):
1) Primary inference path: AWS PrivateLink endpoint -> Redwood NLB -> Redwood Private service in customer-dedicated VPC (or customer-managed ENIs). This preserves cross-account isolation and centralizes control while staying on AWS backbone.
2) Management/control plane: Optional S2S VPN (or Direct Connect) for host provisioning, metrics/collectors, and case escalation; or use a small peered management VPC if the customer is open to limited routing.
3) Fallback: If the customer requires absolute minimum latency and can accept route controls, offer peering as an alternative for production after a security review.

Operational notes / checklist to include in the proposal:
- TLS + mTLS for control channels, cert rotation plan.
- Flow logs and VPC Endpoint policy to restrict who can call the endpoint.
- Autoscaling considerations: how endpoint throughput maps to our NLB targets.
- Monitoring: health check endpoints, path MTU considerations, and packet size tuning for large payloads.
- Failover: multi-AZ NLB + multi-AZ Redwood service, and a documented outage playbook.

Who can produce a customer-ready diagram and a one-page decision table for me to send to Peter? I can draft the security checklist.

Thanks,
Kim
From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 9 Sep 2026 16:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: FW: Connecting our VPC to Redwood Private — options question

Adding a few low-level points to Kim's excellent summary:
- Latency: Peering avoids NLB hop so typically ~5-15ms lower at inter-AZ scale. PrivateLink adds ~1-3ms in-path plus some TCP/ENI overhead depending on NLB config. For our benchmarked models (1k tokens, ~20ms gen time), PrivateLink overhead is negligible for most customers but matters for sub-10ms targets.
- MTU / fragmentation: Our L7 proxy adds headers; recommend 1420-1450 MTU across the path to avoid fragmentation and high CPU overhead on inference hosts. Call this out explicitly for S2S tunnels.
- Health checks: NLB uses TCP health checks; ensure customer's firewall allows the health port (default 8080) and health probe IP ranges.
- BGP vs static: For S2S, encourage BGP for automatic failover; static routes are ok for short-lived PoCs but increase ops toil.

I've attached a rough architecture diagram and a one-pager draft. Please review before we send to Acme.

Attachments: redwood-privatelink-arch.png (image/png)

Subject: Proposed connectivity approach and next steps

Peter — thanks for the call earlier. Attached is our recommended plan and an architecture sketch (see attachments and Drive link). TL;DR recommendation for the pilot:
- Primary: AWS PrivateLink (endpoint service in your VPC pointing to our NLB) for production inference traffic. Rationale: satisfies cross-account isolation policy, stays on AWS backbone, and is straightforward for your security team to audit.
- Management / provisioning: S2S VPN (BGP) for internal orchestration, metrics and administration; keep that channel limited to specific management CIDRs and mTLS-protected.
- Alternative: If Acme's policy team approves limited cross-account routing for a dedicated management VPC, we can discuss a peering option for reduced latency for non-sensitive traffic.

Next steps:
1) I will share the one-pager + diagram (attached) with the Acme security contact.
2) Acme to provide network contacts and endpoint-subnet selection (preferred AZs + subnet IDs).
3) Schedule a 90-minute pilot kickoff (provision small capacity, run perf tests, validate flow logs).

Attachments: redwood-privatelink-arch.png, acme-network-action-plan.xlsx
Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ExampleDesigns

If that aligns, please reply with the network contact and a couple of available times for the kickoff.

Best,
